outcome: No accepted proof of Frankl's conjecture (an element in at least half of the sets of every finite union-closed family) has appeared since 26 January 2024, and the statement is still listed as open in the Wikipedia article I read; in the window the best known universal constant moved from about 0.38271 (Liu, 2023) to about 0.38288525, in two preprints from September 2026 (Costa and Sadhu; Jiang) that give computer-assisted proofs, and the Jiang preprint acknowledges GPT-6 Astra as an AI research assistant; the window also holds restricted-class results (height at most four, chains of at most three sets), a disproof of a weighted variant, and several unrefereed full-proof claims whose status I could not establish.
problem_asks: The bullet asks for one universal claim with three parts. (1) Scope: all families of sets closed under union (sums), i.e. union-closed families. (2) Ground set: the bullet says only 'an element (of the underlying space)'; it does not say finite, and the Wikipedia article I read restricts the conjecture to finite families other than the empty family. For infinite families the literature (Colbert's abstract, as summarised by the fetch) says the statement is false in general, so the finite reading matters; I have taken the finite nonempty reading as the bullet's. (3) Conclusion: some element lies in at least half of the sets of the family (a non-strict fraction of 1/2, not a constant below it). The bullet does not ask for any constant below 1/2, any bound, any particular case, or any counterexample.

events.what_happened: Justin Gilmer, ‘A constant lower bound for the union-closed sets conjecture’ (arXiv 2211.09055). Shows that some element lies in at least a 0.01 fraction of the sets of any union-closed family, via an entropy argument. Gil Kalai's blog reported it on 17 November 2022 (search snippet only).
events.delivers: A constant-fraction bound: an element in at least 0.01 of the sets. A weaker form of the conjecture (the constant is not 1/2).
events.remains: The statement as asked: an element in at least 1/2 of the sets.

checked_by.what_they_did: Blogged 'Amazing: Justin Gilmer gave a constant lower bound for the union-closed sets conjecture' on 17 November 2022. Reported and commented; did not work through the proof in that post as far as the search snippet shows (not opened).

events.time_since_posted: about 4 years; the result was taken up by several groups within days
events.direction: Weaker form: a constant fraction rather than 1/2. Cuts for the conjecture in the sense of a partial result, and does not decide it.

events.what_happened: Zachary Chase and Shachar Lovett, ‘Approximate union closed conjecture’ (arXiv 2211.11689, v1 21 November 2022). The abstract says Gilmer conjectured his technique could be pushed to the constant (3−√5)/2 and that 'We verify his conjecture'. The search summary adds that they show this constant is optimal for approximate union-closed systems.
events.delivers: Constant (3−√5)/2 ≈ 0.382 as a fraction lower bound, verified for Gilmer's entropy inequality (abstract). The search summary reports optimality of this constant for approximate union-closed systems, which is a different setting from exact families.
events.remains: The conjecture's 1/2; the constant is below it.
events.doubts: The optimality claim is from a search summary, not the abstract. The 'approximate' setting is weaker than the exact union-closed statement; I did not read the paper.
events.direction: Constant-fraction bound (≈0.382); cuts for the conjecture only as a partial result.

Abstract: some element is contained in at least (3−√5)/2 ≈ 0.38 of the sets. Published in the Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 31(3) (2024, doi 10.37236/12232), per the reference list of the Jiang preprint.

events.delivers: Some element in at least (3−√5)/2 ≈ 0.38 of the sets of a union-closed family (abstract).
events.remains: The conjecture's 1/2.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in volume 31(3), 2024 (per the Jiang reference list; not opened)

events.direction: Constant-fraction bound (≈0.382); partial, does not decide the 1/2 statement.

events.what_happened: Will Sawin, ‘An improved lower bound for the union-closed set conjecture’ (arXiv 2211.11504, v1 21 November 2022). Raises the proportion from .01 to (3−√5)/2 ≈ .38, and sketches a method that could give a constant strictly greater than this, without a complete proof.
events.delivers: Constant (3−√5)/2 ≈ 0.38 (abstract). A sketched but incomplete route to a larger constant.
events.remains: The conjecture's 1/2.
events.doubts: The method for a larger constant is sketched, not completed (abstract).
events.direction: Constant-fraction bound (≈0.38); partial.

Disproves an entropy inequality route, not the union-closed conjecture. Known only from search summaries of the Lu and Raz note and a search result; not opened.

events.remains: All of the problem.
events.doubts: Not opened; the description is from search results.

The search summaries say Yu evaluated a convex combination of the i.i.d. and max-entropy couplings numerically at about 0.38234. Not opened.

events.what_happened: Stijn Cambie, ‘Better bounds for the union-closed sets conjecture using the entropy approach’ (arXiv 2212.12500, v1 23 December 2022). events.remains: The conjecture's 1/2.
events.direction: Constant-fraction bound; partial.

events.what_happened: Jingbo Liu, ‘Improving the Lower Bound for the Union-closed Sets Conjecture via Conditionally IID Coupling’ (arXiv 2306.08824, submitted 15 June 2023). Gives a lower bound of about 0.38271 under hypotheses that were checked numerically rather than proved. Wikipedia cites this figure (opened), and Lu and Raz name it the best known constant (2024). The arXiv page itself was not opened; the figure comes from search summaries and the Wikipedia article.

events.remains: The conjecture's 1/2; and the hypotheses behind 0.38271 are numerical, not proved.

events.what_happened: Theophilus Agama, ‘A proof of the union-close set conjecture’ (arXiv 1711.02665). Introduces universes, induced communities and spots, and claims that for any finite universe and induced community some spot has density at least 1/2. v1 7 November 2017; v4 11 March 2021; v6 9 March 2026 (latest), described as a reformatting with an expanded introduction, 'ideas remain unchanged'.
events.revisions: v1 7 Nov 2017; v2 9 Nov 2017; v3 10 Nov 2017; v4 11 Mar 2021; v5 21 Apr 2021; v6 9 Mar 2026 (reformatted, introduction expanded, ideas unchanged).

events.remains: Nothing, by its own claim; the mapping to the problem is not shown on the abstract page.
events.time_since_posted: about 9 years; latest version March 2026 with no uptake found
events.doubts: No review, journal or independent verification shown. The v4 text (2021) is said by a search summary to still call the conjecture open; I did not open that version. Full text not read.
events.direction: Claims the conjecture, so cuts for it if correct.

events.what_happened: Roberts and Simpson (2010) verified the conjecture for families of at most 50 sets; Vuckovic and Zivkovic (2017) combined this with their own work to the same bound (Wikipedia). Listed on Wikipedia; the original paper was not opened.
events.delivers: The conjecture holds for union-closed families with at most 50 sets (finitely many instances of a universal claim; per §2.1 this does not move the statement, though it is a restricted class).
events.remains: All families with more than 50 sets.
events.doubts: From the Wikipedia list only; not opened.
events.direction: Restricted class (family size); cuts for the conjecture only within that class.

events.what_happened: Vuckovic and Zivkovic (2017) verified the conjecture for families whose ground set has at most 12 elements (Wikipedia, which also names Bošnjak–Marković 2008, Morris 2006 and Lo Faro 1994 as earlier bounds). Listed on Wikipedia; the original was not opened.
events.delivers: The conjecture for union-closed families on at most 12 ground elements (a restricted class by universe size).
events.remains: Universes with more than 12 elements.
events.doubts: From the Wikipedia list only; not opened.
events.direction: Restricted class (universe size); cuts for the conjecture only within that class.

events.what_happened: Sarvate and Renaud (1989) proved the conjecture when the smallest set has one or two elements; later rediscovered by others (Wikipedia). Not opened.
events.delivers: The conjecture when the smallest set in the family has one or two elements (restricted class).
events.remains: Families whose smallest set has three or more elements.
events.doubts: From the Wikipedia list only; not opened.
events.direction: Restricted class; cuts for the conjecture within that class only.

events.what_happened: Ilan Karpas (2017), an unpublished preprint, proves the conjecture for dense families: at least (1/2 − ε)·2^n subsets of an n-element set, for some constant ε > 0 (Wikipedia). Gil Kalai's blog covered the proof in March 2018 (search snippet only). Not opened.
events.delivers: The conjecture for families containing a (1/2 − ε) fraction of all subsets of the ground set (restricted, dense class).
events.remains: Sparser families.
events.doubts: Unpublished per Wikipedia. Not opened.
events.direction: Restricted (dense) class; cuts for the conjecture only within that class.

events.what_happened: Bruhn et al. (2015) show that the graph (bipartite) formulation of the conjecture holds for chordal bipartite graphs, series-parallel graphs and graphs of maximum degree three (Wikipedia). Not opened.
events.delivers: A reformulation (bipartite graphs) holds for three graph classes; this is a restricted class of a reformulation, not the statement.
events.remains: The conjecture for general graphs and for families outside these classes.
events.doubts: From the Wikipedia list only; not opened.
events.direction: Restricted classes of a reformulation; cuts for the reformulation within those classes.

events.what_happened: Chenxiao Tian (2021), ‘Union-closed Sets Conjecture Holds for Height No More Than 3 and Height No Less Than N-1’ (arXiv 2112.06659, identifier suggests December 2021; not opened). Wikipedia states the chain-height result (opened).
events.delivers: The conjecture for families of height at most 3 or at least n−1 (height of the inclusion poset), per Wikipedia and the title.
events.remains: Families of intermediate height, including height 4 and 5 (taken up in 2026 by Tian, see tian-2026).
events.doubts: Not opened.
events.direction: Restricted class (height); cuts for the conjecture within that class.

events.what_happened: The lattice form of the conjecture is known for several subclasses: Poonen (1992), Abe (2000), Reinhold (2000) (Wikipedia). Bundled here; not opened.
events.delivers: The lattice version for several subclasses of lattices (restricted classes of a reformulation).
events.remains: The lattice version in general and the set-family version.
events.doubts: From the Wikipedia list only; not opened. Bundled because the three papers are cited together there.
events.direction: Restricted classes of a reformulation.

events.what_happened: Abigail Raz (2017) gave a counterexample to a question from the Polymath-era project: whether every family satisfying Reimer's conditions meets the abundance condition. The counterexample has n = 8 and |S| = 11 (per a search summary; the Lu and Raz abstract, opened, confirms only that Raz gave a minimal counterexample). Raz's paper was not opened.
events.delivers: Disproves a Reimer-conditions question (a different question about families satisfying Reimer's conditions), not the union-closed conjecture.
events.remains: The union-closed conjecture; the disproved question is a different statement.
events.doubts: The 2017 date and the n = 8, |S| = 11 figures come from search summaries; the Lu–Raz abstract (opened) does not give them. Raz's paper not opened.
events.direction: Neutral to the conjecture; disproves a different statement.
events.object: A family with n = 8 and |S| = 11 satisfying Reimer's conditions but not the abundance condition (per a search summary). Not a counterexample to the union-closed conjecture, which asks for abundance of a union-closed family.

events.what_happened: Jonad Pulaj, ‘Cutting planes for families implying Frankl's conjecture’ (Mathematics of Computation, epub 25 July 2019). A computational method finds previously unknown families of sets that imply the conjecture (for all union-closed families containing them), and answers a 2006 conjecture of Morris in the negative (per the repository abstract, opened).
events.revisions: First public version date is not established beyond the journal's epub date; an earlier preprint may exist and was not checked.
events.delivers: Finds classes of families for which the conjecture is implied (via Poonen's theorem and explicit weights); also a counterexample to a conjecture of Morris (per the repository abstract). The number of families found is not stated.
events.remains: The conjecture for all union-closed families.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published (epub ahead of print, per the repository record)

machine_checked.system: Computer-based cutting-plane search (not a proof assistant)

events.direction: Finds implying classes (restricted sufficiency results) and a counterexample to a different conjecture of Morris; does not settle the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Roberto Demontis, ‘The union-closed set conjecture is true’ (arXiv 2405.03731, v1 6 May 2024). Abstract (opened, truncated on the page): 'We prove that the conjecture made by Peter Frankl in the late 1970s is true', stated as: every finite union-closed family containing a nonempty set has an element in at least half of its members. Only v1 listed.
events.revisions: v1 only (6 May 2024), per the arXiv page.
events.delivers: Claims the full conjecture as stated (every finite union-closed family containing a nonempty set has an element in at least half of its members).
events.remains: Nothing, by its own claim.
events.doubts: The abstract is truncated and does not describe the method. No comments, no later version, no journal, no review. Searches found no expert engagement. The full text was not read.
events.direction: Claims the conjecture, so cuts for it if correct.

events.what_happened: Kengbo Lu and Abigail Raz, ‘Note on the union-closed sets conjecture and Reimer's average set size theorem’ (arXiv 2405.10639, v1 17 May 2024, v2 30 May 2024). States that the conjecture 'remains an open problem in discrete mathematics'. Gives a general method for infinitely many counterexamples to a Reimer-conditions question (different question) and discusses how far they are from being union-closed.
events.revisions: v1 17 May 2024; v2 30 May 2024 (current).
events.delivers: A statement that the conjecture is open (abstract), and counterexamples to a Reimer-conditions question. Neither moves the conjecture. The search summary says the note cites 0.38271 as the best known constant; the abstract does not.
events.remains: All of the conjecture.
events.doubts: The Reimer-conditions counterexamples concern a different question; I did not read the full text.

events.object: Infinitely many families satisfying Reimer's conditions but failing the abundance condition, by a general construction (per the abstract). These answer a different question; they are not counterexamples to the union-closed conjecture.

events.what_happened: Veronica Phan, ‘Entropy approach for a generalization of Frankl's conjecture’ (arXiv 2412.18622, v1 17 December 2024; the only version listed). Abstract: uses the entropy approach 'to derive a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of an element that belongs to at least half of the sets' of a finite family. The condition is not stated in the abstract.
events.delivers: Claims a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of an element in at least half of the sets of a finite family. The condition is not stated in the abstract, so I cannot tell whether it is a restatement of the conjecture or a sufficient case of it.
events.remains: Unknown until the condition and its proof are read.
events.doubts: The condition is not stated; the title says 'generalization', but the abstract concerns the existence statement itself. Full text not read.

events.what_happened: Shagnik Das and Saintan Wu, ‘Frequent elements in union-closed set families’ (arXiv 2412.03862, v1 5 December 2024; v3 11 July 2025). Proves Nagel's conjecture for every k ≥ 2 (the kth most popular element lies in at least 1/(2^(k−1)+1) of the sets) and characterises the extremal families. As the family size grows, the kth most popular element lies in at least ((3−√5)/2 − o(1)) of the sets.
events.revisions: v1 5 Dec 2024; v2 14 Dec 2024; v3 11 Jul 2025 ('Simplified and strengthened our proofs to obtain Nagel's conjecture in full').
events.delivers: Nagel's generalisation for k ≥ 2 (the second-, third- and later most popular elements), and the asymptotic constant (3−√5)/2 − o(1) for the kth most popular element. The k = 1 case, which is the union-closed conjecture, is not proved.
events.remains: The k = 1 case (the conjecture itself).
events.doubts: The k ≥ 2 results are not the conjecture; the k = 1 case is named as the conjecture and left open.
events.direction: Moves a generalised quantity (the kth most popular element); does not settle k = 1, the conjecture's own quantity.

events.what_happened: Cory H. Colbert, ‘Chain Conditions and Optimal Elements in Generalized Union-Closed Families of Sets’ (arXiv 2412.18740, v1 25 December 2024; v3 2 December 2025). Abstract: 'the union-closed conjecture holds for both finite and infinite union-closed families' in which every chain of sets has cardinality at most three; also covers nontrivial topological spaces with the descending chain condition. A 2026 paper cites it as Order 43 (2026), article 5 (from that citation; the journal page was not opened).
events.revisions: v1 25 Dec 2024; v2 1 Jan 2025; v3 2 Dec 2025 (13 pages, 5 figures). Journal: Order 43 (2026); the search summary gives acceptance 10 Nov 2025 and publication 8 Dec 2025 (not opened).
events.delivers: The conjecture for finite union-closed families with every chain of at most three sets; for infinite families of the same kind; and for certain topological spaces. The abstract states that the conjecture is false in the infinite setting in general, so the restriction matters.
events.remains: Union-closed families with a chain of four or more sets (other than the topological cases).

events.what_happened: Ze-Chun Hu, Yi-Ding Shi and Qian-Qian Zhou, ‘A lemma on a finite union-closed family of finite sets and its applications’ (arXiv 2507.11008, v1 15 July 2025; v2 1 September 2025). A frequency lemma: if a fraction c of the sets of the reduced family G contain j, then at least c/(2−c) of the sets of F do. The applications are not named in the abstract.

events.what_happened: Christopher Bouchard, ‘On the lattice formulation of the union-closed sets conjecture’ (arXiv 2503.00277, v1 1 March 2025). Restates the conjecture for finite lattices (a join-irreducible element below at most half of the elements) and derives necessary conditions for any minimum-size counterexample. Journal reference on arXiv: Le Matematiche 81(1) (2026), pp. 153–165.
events.revisions: v1 1 Mar 2025 only; journal reference Le Matematiche 81(1), 2026.

events.remains: The conjecture, in both the lattice and the set-family forms.
events.direction: Neutral: a reformulation with necessary conditions on any counterexample.

events.what_happened: Christopher Bouchard, ‘An averaging result for union-closed families of sets’ (arXiv 2509.12537, v1 16 September 2025). Proves that for separating union-closed families of height h = 4 with |B| ≤ 2 (B a smallest irredundant generating subfamily of size less than n/2), the average member size is at least n/2. Shows height 4 is the largest for which this works, and treats 3 ≤ |B| ≤ 4.
events.revisions: v1 16 Sep 2025 only.
events.delivers: An average-size bound for a restricted class (separating families of height 4, |B| ≤ 2). The conjecture asks for an element in half the sets, not an average set size; the abstract does not connect the two.
events.remains: The conjecture for general union-closed families.
events.doubts: Different statement (average size, restricted class); the abstract does not say it advances the conjecture.
events.direction: Averaging bound on a restricted class; a different question from the conjecture as asked.

events.what_happened: Masahiro Hachimori and Kenji Kashiwabara, ‘On the Averaging Problem of Ideal Families Related to Frankl's Conjecture with Formal Proof by Lean 4’ (arXiv 2504.13454, v1 18 April 2025). Restates Frankl's conjecture for intersection-closed families. Proves that the normalised degree sum of every ideal family is nonpositive ('average rarity'), which implies a rare vertex. Says the proof is formalised and verified in Lean 4.
events.revisions: v1 18 Apr 2025 only.
events.delivers: For ideal families (downward-closed families), an average-rarity result: normalised degree sum nonpositive, giving a rare vertex. This is a restricted class (ideal families), in the intersection-closed form of the conjecture.
events.remains: The conjecture for general union-closed (intersection-closed) families.

events.doubts: The Lean claim is from the abstract; sorry status and statement not checked.

events.what_happened: Masahiro Hachimori and Kenji Kashiwabara, ‘Average-Rare Order Ideals in Functional Preorders’ (arXiv 2511.19833, v1 25 November 2025). Shows that the order ideals of the preorder induced by a function are average-rare (normalised degree sum nonpositive); proves the base case for rooted forests; proposes a conjecture 'related to' Frankl's conjecture; states that all proofs are verified in Lean 4.

events.delivers: Average-rarity for order ideals of functional preorders. Does not prove anything about the union-closed or intersection-closed conjecture; it proposes a related conjecture.
events.remains: The conjecture, and the proposed related conjecture (not stated on the abstract page).
events.doubts: The related conjecture is not stated on the abstract page. Lean claim not checked.
events.direction: Neutral on the conjecture: a different family class and a proposed related conjecture.

events.what_happened: Jamolidin K. Abdurakhmanov, ‘On the existence of heavy columns in binary matrices with distinct rows’ (arXiv 2601.18450, submitted 26 January 2026). Two recursive algorithms; Theorems 1 and 2 say the matrices they accept contain a heavy column (at least m/2 ones). The abstract and metadata do not mention union-closed families or Frankl's conjecture. A reformulation of the conjecture (Roos) concerns a heavy-column statement for a matrix of a union-closed family, so the link is by analogy only.

events.delivers: Heavy-column theorems for binary matrices with distinct rows, under the algorithms' acceptance conditions. The paper, per its abstract, does not state a union-closed consequence.
events.remains: The conjecture; no link is established in the abstract.
events.doubts: A heavy-column statement is an analogue of the conjecture's matrix form; the paper does not claim it. Full text not read.
events.direction: Neutral: an analogous heavy-column statement, no claim about the conjecture.

events.what_happened: A ResearchGate record, ‘(PDF) An algorithmic proof of Frankl's union-closed sets conjecture’ (publication 400159567), by Jamolidin K. Abdurakhmanov, upload date 28 January 2026 (per a search snippet). The ResearchGate page returned HTTP 403 and was not opened. Two search snippets describe it differently: one as a complete proof of the full conjecture, linking union-closed families to binary matrices and the heavy-column result above; the other as proving the case |⋃F| ≤ 11, which is narrower.
events.delivers: Unresolved. Either a claimed full proof, or a claim for union size at most 11 (only the snippets say which).
events.remains: Unknown until the document is read.
events.doubts: Not opened (HTTP 403). Two incompatible snippet descriptions. No expert engagement found.
events.direction: Unresolved: a claim whose scope is unknown from my sources.

events.what_happened: Boon Suan Ho, ‘A generalization of Boppana's entropy inequality’ (arXiv 2601.19327, submitted 27 January 2026). Proves α_k·h(x^k) ≥ x^(k−1)·h(x) for all real k > 1 (a version Yuster conjectured), where h is binary entropy and α_k the positive solution of x(1+x)^(k−1) = 1. Gives an analogue of the union-closed conjecture for approximate k-union-closed systems. The paper states it formalises the proof in Lean 4.
events.revisions: v1 27 Jan 2026 only.
events.delivers: An analogue for approximate k-union-closed systems (k > 1). The abstract makes no claim for k = 1, the original conjecture; Boppana's inequality is the k = 2 case.
events.remains: The original conjecture (k = 1) and the exact union-closed statement.
events.doubts: The Lean claim is from the abstract; not checked. The analogue is a different question (approximate k > 1).
events.direction: Neutral on k = 1: a generalisation to a different question.

events.what_happened: Reed, Jonathan ƒ(n), ‘The Reflection Restored: A Machine-Certified Proof of Frankl's Conjecture via Collision-Restitution Invariants’ (Zenodo 19441515, v1, 6 April 2026, CC BY 4.0). Claims that a 'collision-restitution invariant' verified in Lean 4 gives that 0.5 is the minimum density for a union-closed family and so proves the conjecture. Files: Frankl's_Conjecture_Proof.lean and a PDF. A GitHub repository (AEjonanonymous/Union-Closed-Sets-Conjecture) carries the same claim: 'a structural invariant verified in Lean 4', verification status 'No goals', and the file listing. The README and Zenodo page carry the topic tag 'ai-augmented-research' and the GitHub listing has a file named Gemini_Generated_Image_....
events.revisions: Zenodo v1.0 (6 April 2026). The GitHub repo has 37 commits with no dates visible.
events.delivers: Claims a complete proof (for the full statement, per the Zenodo abstract and the README). The Lean statement displayed in the README (restitution_exists) asserts only that for any two members of a union-closed F there is some member of F. Per the fetch's reading, union-closure gives this directly, and the displayed statement does not visibly give the frequency claim.
events.remains: Unknown: the 0.5 claim is not shown formally in the displayed README excerpt.
events.directly_checkable: The Lean file Frankl's_Conjecture_Proof.lean in the GitHub repo and the Zenodo record; neither file's contents were read, so the sorry count and whether the 0.5 step is formalised are unknown.
events.doubts: The displayed key theorem looks weaker than the claim (as the fetch noted). Repo has 1 star and no visible review. The Zenodo record is a self-published preprint. The 'Gemini_Generated_Image' filename and the 'ai-augmented-research' tag name a system only in a figure or a tag; no sentence says what it did. Lean file not read.
events.direction: Claims the conjecture, so cuts for it if correct.
people: Jonathan Reed (listed as Reed, Jonathan ƒ(n))

events.what_happened: Yunjiang Jiang, ‘Entropy bounds and global couplings for union-closed families’ (arXiv 2609.08291, v1 8 September 2026, single version, math.CO, CC BY 4.0). Main result (Theorem 1.1): every finite union-closed family containing a nonempty set has an element p with p ≥ 1531541/4000000 = 0.38288525, where p is the largest element frequency. The abstract calls the proof 'computer-assisted'; Section 9 and Appendix B describe outward-rounded interval arithmetic over rectangles and squares, with the verification program in Appendix B. Also an entropy gain over independent sampling and a size-dependent frequency bound (explicit form not read). The author footnote reads 'AI research assistance: GPT-6.' and the acknowledgements read 'GPT-6 Astra served as an AI assistant in the research and preparation of this manuscript' and 'Part of this research was carried out at Axiom Math'. The paper's reference [9] is Costa's single-author Zenodo preprint (doi 10.5281/zenodo.22072655, 2026).
events.revisions: v1 8 Sep 2026 only.
events.delivers: A constant-fraction lower bound 0.38288525 on the largest element frequency in any finite union-closed family containing a nonempty set; plus a size-dependent bound (not read). It is a weaker form of the conjecture, which asks for 1/2. The bound is below 1/2 and so does not establish the conjecture.
events.remains: The conjecture's 1/2: the paper proves ≈0.3829, not 1/2.
events.time_since_posted: about 1 month; no human engagement found

machine_checked.system: In-house outward-rounded interval arithmetic program (Appendix B; Python per a PDF reading; author not stated)

events.directly_checkable: The interval verification program is described in Section 9 and Appendix B and is reportedly embedded in the PDF as base64. Its author and any public release are not stated; I did not decode or run it.
events.doubts: (a) A computer-assisted proof whose program's authorship is not stated; the main theorem 'depends on' the verification (Section 9 text). (b) The bound is numerically precise to eight digits and was posted one day after Costa and Sadhu's joint paper gave the same bound (see disputes). (c) The paper's own reference to Costa's earlier, weaker preprint, and the AI-assisted role, are not explained. (d) Not refereed; no expert engagement found in searches.
events.direction: Cuts for a weaker form (a constant lower bound, 0.38288525 < 1/2). It moves the best known constant but does not settle the conjecture.

systems.name: GPT-6 Astra
systems.what_it_did: Per the authors, served as an AI assistant in the research and preparation of the manuscript. The footnote names 'GPT-6'. The paper does not say what the assistant produced: no statement attributes the theorem, the proof, the interval program or the write-up to it. Whether its input was load-bearing for the 0.38288525 bound is not stated.
systems.basis_quote: GPT-6 Astra served as an AI assistant in the research and preparation of this manuscript.

events.what_happened: Simone Costa (University of Brescia), ‘Beyond Liu's 0.382709 threshold for the union-closed sets conjecture’, single-author Zenodo preprint 22072655 (v1, 23 August 2026). Claims c_UC ≥ c_L and then c_UC ≥ c_L + 2·10⁻⁵, where c_L is Liu's threshold (above 0.382709087918735). The record says this manuscript has since been incorporated into the joint paper with Ankan Sadhu (Zenodo 22727713).
events.revisions: v1 23 Aug 2026 (single author); incorporated into the joint Costa–Sadhu paper.
events.delivers: A lower bound c_L + 2·10⁻⁵ ≈ 0.38272 on the constant (a weaker form). Its claimed improvement is below the 0.38288525 of the joint paper and of Jiang.
events.remains: The conjecture's 1/2.
events.time_since_posted: about 7 weeks; superseded by the joint paper
events.doubts: Superseded by the joint paper, per the record. Its bound is a lower bound on the constant; the Zenodo record was read, not the PDF.
events.direction: Constant-fraction bound (≈0.38272); partial.

events.what_happened: Simone Costa (University of Brescia) and Ankan Sadhu (Government College of Engineering & Ceramic Technology), ‘Beyond Liu's 0.382709 threshold for the union-closed sets conjecture’, joint paper. Zenodo 22727713 (version v3, first made public 7 September 2026; the Zenodo record is dated 12 September 2026). arXiv 2610.02295 (submitted 1 October 2026, math.CO). Abstract: 'c_UC ≥ 0.3828852549667978', where c_UC is the largest universal lower bound on the proportion of sets sharing an element; combines an independent protocol with Liu's Example 5 and optimises coefficients. It states that the inequality used cannot yield a threshold above about 0.38288526. The computational supplement uses certified interval evaluations (Appendix A; Section 5 and Section 6 text).
events.revisions: Zenodo 22727713 v3 first public 7 Sep 2026 (title, abstract and introduction updated, results unchanged per Zenodo notes); arXiv 2610.02295 v1 1 Oct 2026. The arXiv comments say the first version was posted on Zenodo on 7 September 2026.
events.delivers: A lower bound c_UC ≥ 0.3828852549667978, computer-assisted with certified interval evaluations, on the best universal constant. It does not claim 1/2.
events.remains: The conjecture's 1/2; the paper states the method cannot go above about 0.38288526.

machine_checked.system: Certified interval evaluations in the computational supplement (Appendix A); not a proof assistant

events.directly_checkable: The computational supplement and ancillary zip on Zenodo 22727713 (files costa_sadhu_union_closed_computational_supplementV3.pdf and ancillaryV3.zip). Not opened.
events.doubts: Computer-assisted with interval evaluations; not refereed; no expert engagement found. I read about 100k of the arXiv HTML's 129k characters. The arXiv HTML shows no acknowledgement or AI statement in what I read, and the Zenodo record states no AI or LLM use.
events.direction: Cuts for a weaker form (constant lower bound 0.38288525 < 1/2); no claim on 1/2.

events.what_happened: Yimeng Wang, ‘The weighted union-set conjecture is false’ (arXiv 2609.25101, v1 19 September 2026). Abstract: disproves a weighted generalisation of the union-set conjecture [Fra95] raised in [Gow16]; constructs nonnegative weights on subsets of a finite ground set with w(∅) = 0 and w(A∪B) ≥ min{w(A), w(B)}, such that each coordinate carries only an arbitrarily small fraction of the total weight. The reference list cites Jiang's entropy preprint (per search summary). The PDF was unreadable to my tools.
events.revisions: v1 19 Sep 2026 only.
events.delivers: A weighted version (with weights and a min-type union condition) in which no single element carries more than an arbitrarily small share. Per the abstract it disproves a weighted analogue of the union-set conjecture. It is not the unweighted statement.
events.remains: The unweighted conjecture, and whether the unweighted union-set conjecture [Fra95] is the union-closed conjecture is not established from what I could read.
events.doubts: Whether the 'union-set conjecture [Fra95]' is the same statement as the union-closed conjecture is not shown; the PDF could not be read. The counterexample is a weighted one, which is a different question.
events.direction: Disproves a weighted analogue; neutral on the unweighted statement as far as I can establish.
events.object: A nonnegative weight function on subsets of a finite ground set, with w(∅) = 0 and the min-type union condition, where each element carries an arbitrarily small share of the total weight (per the abstract). Explicit or existence-only not stated on the abstract page.

events.what_happened: Chenxiao Tian, ‘Frankl's Conjecture at Height Four and the Structure of Height-Five Counterexamples’ (arXiv 2608.25147, v1 25 August 2026, 18 pages). Proves the conjecture for finite union-closed families of height at most four; for height five, assumes a smallest counterexample and derives structural constraints (even cardinality 2t, at least three critical elements, t ≥ 2n−1), leaving a 'remaining transfer problem' open.
events.revisions: v1 25 Aug 2026 only.
events.delivers: The conjecture for finite union-closed families of height at most four (an unconditional restricted-class result, in the empty-set-free form per the abstract). Height five is not resolved.
events.remains: Height five and above, and the general conjecture; the author's structural results are conditional on a hypothetical counterexample.
events.doubts: Restricted class. Equivalence of the height-four statement with the at-least-half form is per the abstract. Full text not read; no expert engagement found.
events.direction: Proves the conjecture within a restricted class (height at most four). Cuts for the conjecture within that class.

events.what_happened: Aaronson, Ellis and Leader (2021) proved a special case of the union-closed conjecture; the case is described in the Koutsoukou-Argyraki and Paulson abstract as a 2021 proof, and a search summary says it concerns families generated by cyclic translates of a fixed set. The original 2021 paper was not opened.
events.delivers: Per search summaries: the conjecture for the union-closed family generated by the cyclic translates of a fixed set (restricted class, unverified).
events.remains: The general conjecture.
events.doubts: The class is from a search summary, not the abstract. Original paper not opened.
events.direction: Restricted class; cuts for the conjecture within that class.

disputes.summary: Costa and Sadhu's joint paper (Zenodo 22727713, v3 first public 7 September 2026; arXiv 2610.02295, 1 October 2026) and Jiang's preprint (arXiv 2609.08291, 8 September 2026) give the same bound to eight digits: 0.3828852549667978 (Costa–Sadhu) and 1531541/4000000 = 0.38288525 (Jiang). Jiang's reference [9] cites Costa's single-author Zenodo preprint of 23 August 2026 (doi 10.5281/zenodo.22072655), which has a weaker bound (c_L + 2·10⁻⁵). Who first had the 0.38288525 argument, and whether the two are independent, is not established by what I read: I did not find a statement in either text about the other's result, and Costa–Sadhu's visible text does not cite Jiang. Jiang's footnote credits GPT-6 Astra as an AI assistant; Costa–Sadhu's visible text has no AI statement.

The ResearchGate 'algorithmic proof of Frankl's union-closed sets conjecture' (Abdurakhmanov, January 2026) is described in one search snippet as a complete proof of the full conjecture, and in another as a proof for union size at most 11. The page was not opened (HTTP 403), so the scope is unresolved.

Several unrefereed full-proof claims exist with no public engagement found: Blinovsky and Speranca (2015; v11 2024-09-11), Agama (2017; v6 2026-03-09), Demontis (2024), Reed (2026, Lean repository), and the ResearchGate claim above. Scandone (2023), Schäge (2016) and Acquaah Peter (2018) are withdrawn. None of the live claims has an accepted verification in my sources.

summary: Searches and reads over 2022–2026 find no accepted resolution of the conjecture as stated (an element in at least half the sets of every finite union-closed family). The Wikipedia article I read (current, not the frozen January 2024 text) still calls it open and says the best known constant is about 0.38271, citing Liu (2023) and Lu–Raz (2024); Lu and Raz's note itself says the conjecture 'remains an open problem'. Within the window the constant moved on the two sides of a single number. On 7–8 September 2026 two papers, by Costa and Sadhu (joint Zenodo v3, 7 September; arXiv 2610.02295, 1 October) and by Jiang (arXiv 2609.08291, 8 September), give c ≥ 0.38288525 by computer-assisted interval arithmetic. Each proves a constant below 1/2 and claims nothing at 1/2. The Jiang paper is the only event I found that names an AI system: its acknowledgements say 'GPT-6 Astra served as an AI assistant in the research and preparation of this manuscript' and its footnote says 'AI research assistance: GPT-6'. The paper does not say what the assistant produced, and it does not say who wrote the interval verification program on which the theorem depends; that makes the AI's role unclear, not absent. The Costa–Sadhu paper states no AI use in what I read. I checked the OpenAI 'ten advances' list, through the openai/ten-proofs README (the OpenAI post itself returned HTTP 403): its ten results do not include any union-closed result, and I found no other AI-linked union-closed result. Restricted-class results in the window are Colbert (chains of at most three sets, finite and infinite; published in Order), and Tian (height at most four, 25 August 2026; height five open). Several 2024–2026 papers treat related but different questions: Das and Wu (Nagel's generalisation, k ≥ 2), Wang (a weighted analogue disproved), Bouchard (average size on height-4 families), Hachimori and Kashiwabara (ideal families, Lean-checked), Ho (approximate k > 1), Hu–Shi–Zhou (a frequency lemma), and Koutsoukou-Argyraki and Paulson (Isabelle formalisation of a 2021 special case). Unrefereed full-proof claims in the window are Demontis (May 2024, abstract only), Reed (April 2026, Lean repository whose key theorem looks weaker than the claim, sorry status unknown) and the ResearchGate paper (January 2026, unresolved). Close calls: (i) whether the Jiang and Costa–Sadhu bound is one event or two, and which date the constant's status rests on (both are in the first week of September 2026, a day apart); (ii) whether the Jiang AI acknowledgement is load-bearing, since the paper says the theorem depends on the computer verification but does not attribute that verification to the AI; (iii) whether Colbert's chain-of-three result is 'in the statement' or a restricted class, since the bullet asks for all finite union-closed families; (iv) whether Phan (2024) gives a restatement of the conjecture, since its characterising condition is not stated in the abstract I read.
competing_reading: Read the Jiang preprint as a genuine AI-assisted contribution: a named model is credited in the acknowledgements with 'research and preparation', the main theorem is computer-assisted and the authors say the theorem depends on the verification, and the same acknowledgements say part of the research was carried out at Axiom Math (the record does not establish Axiom Math's role). On that reading the AI system did load-bearing work on the constant. The opposite reading: the constant bound is a weaker form, the AI sentence is generic and names no specific output, and the authors credit the assistant in the same way they would credit a tool. The judging pass should weigh the mismatch: 'research and preparation' does not say the assistant wrote the interval program or derived the bound. Separately, the constant bound could be read as moving the statement's quantity (the largest element frequency) without moving the 1/2 threshold; read that way it is a partial result and not a resolution.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The full Jiang text (the part after 100k characters in the HTML, including Appendix B and the author's own description of what the assistant did), or a statement from the author on which steps GPT-6 Astra produced. (2) Who wrote the interval program, and whether it is public (Jiang Appendix B, and any Zenodo or GitHub release). (3) Whether Costa and Sadhu had Jiang's preprint or the reverse, from version histories or correspondence; the Jiang reference to Costa's 22072655 record and the Costa–Sadhu v3 change of title and abstract would help. (4) Independent recomputation of the interval verification for 0.38288525 by a specialist. (5) For Demontis, Blinovsky–Speranca v11, Agama v6, Reed and the ResearchGate paper: a journal acceptance, an expert write-up, or a retraction. (6) For the 1/2 statement itself: an argument that reaches 1/2 and survives review, or a counterexample.

event.what_happened: Cory H. Colbert, ‘Chain Conditions and Optimal Elements in Generalized Union-Closed Families of Sets’ (arXiv 2412.18740, v1 25 December 2024; v3 2 December 2025). Abstract: 'the union-closed conjecture holds for both finite and infinite union-closed families' in which every chain of sets has cardinality at most three; also covers nontrivial topological spaces with the descending chain condition. A 2026 paper cites it as Order 43 (2026), article 5 (from that citation; the journal page was not opened).
event.revisions: v1 25 Dec 2024; v2 1 Jan 2025; v3 2 Dec 2025 (13 pages, 5 figures). Journal: Order 43 (2026); the search summary gives acceptance 10 Nov 2025 and publication 8 Dec 2025 (not opened).
event.delivers: The conjecture for finite union-closed families with every chain of at most three sets; for infinite families of the same kind; and for certain topological spaces. The abstract states that the conjecture is false in the infinite setting in general, so the restriction matters.
event.remains: Union-closed families with a chain of four or more sets (other than the topological cases).

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper (per search summary of the journal page; not opened)

event.doubts: The 'chains of at most three sets' condition is a cardinality bound on chains, per the abstract; the search summary notes it may differ from chain length convention. Journal status from a search summary.
event.direction: Proves the conjecture within a restricted class (chains of at most three sets, finite and infinite). Cuts for the conjecture within that class.

judgement.why: The statement asks for an element in at least half the sets of every (finite) union-closed family, so constant-fraction results below 1/2 are bounds (F4), and restricted classes (height at most four, chains of at most three sets, ideal families, small smallest set, dense families) are cases. Within the window the live full-proof claims (Demontis, Reed, the ResearchGate paper) are not_credible: each has no uptake on a landmark problem, later papers in the window still call the conjecture open, and each has its own aggravating signal (Reed's displayed Lean theorem is trivial, and the ResearchGate claim describes its own scope inconsistently). Blinovsky–Speranca and Agama are dated by first posting because their window revisions show no new mathematics. Colbert counts as digested because Order accepted it. Jiang's AI credit is the close call. The quote 'GPT-6 Astra served as an AI assistant in the research and preparation of this manuscript' does not say the model produced any argument, construction or bound, and the record finds no statement attributing the theorem or the interval program to it. Read on the quote alone, that is too thin to be mathematics in the result, so ai_role is none. Jiang is also marked doubtful because it gives the same eight-digit constant a day after Costa–Sadhu.
judgement.doubts: Jiang's AI role could become 'assisted' if the unread part of the paper (after 100k characters) or the author says GPT-6 Astra produced the coupling, the bound or the interval program; the 'Axiom Math' acknowledgement is unexplained. Priority between Costa–Sadhu (7 September 2026) and Jiang (8 September 2026) on 0.38288525 is unresolved. Phan 2024 and van der Hout–Roos 2026 were scored none because their content is unknown, not because they were shown to be empty. Colbert's journal acceptance rests on a search summary of the Order page. The Hachimori–Kashiwabara ideal-family result is in the intersection-closed form; it was treated as an equivalent restricted class.
